# The Lorentzian family $\delta_n(x)=\dfrac n\pi\dfrac1{1+n^2x^2}$ is a delta sequence

## Statement

For $n \in \mathbb{N}_{>0}$ define $\delta_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$$\delta_n(x) \;:=\; \frac n \pi \, \frac 1 {1 + n^2 x^2}.$$
Then $\langle \delta_n\rangle_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}}$ is a delta sequence: in the sense of distributions,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\delta_n = \delta ,$$
that is, for every test function $\phi \in \mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R}) = C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R})$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,\phi(x)\,dx \;=\; \delta(\phi) \;=\; \phi(0).$$

## Conventions and preliminaries

$\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$ denotes the space of test functions on $\mathbb{R}$: the infinitely differentiable functions
$\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$ whose support $\operatorname{supp}\phi$ is a compact subset of $\mathbb{R}$.
The Dirac delta distribution is the linear functional $\delta:\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})\to\mathbb{C}$, $\delta(\phi)=\phi(0)$.

A sequence $(T_n)$ of distributions converges to a distribution $T$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$ iff
$T_n(\phi)\to T(\phi)$ for every $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$; this is exactly the assertion displayed above.

Each $\delta_n$ is a continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$ (its denominator $1+n^2x^2 \ge 1$ never vanishes), hence
locally integrable, hence it defines a regular distribution
$$T_{\delta_n}(\phi) \;=\; \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx ,$$
the integral being effectively taken over the compact set $\operatorname{supp}\phi$, so that it exists
as a Riemann (equivalently Lebesgue) integral of a continuous compactly supported integrand.
We abbreviate $T_{\delta_n}$ by $\delta_n$, as usual.

All integrals of $\delta_n$ alone below are absolutely convergent improper Riemann integrals, which
coincide with the corresponding Lebesgue integrals because the integrands are continuous and
nonnegative.

Throughout, for $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$ we write
$$\|\phi\|_\infty := \sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}} |\phi(x)|,$$
which is finite: $\phi$ is continuous and vanishes outside a compact set $K$, so $|\phi|$ attains a
finite maximum on $K$ and is $0$ off $K$.

## Lemma 1 (normalisation)

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}_{>0}$,
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx \;=\; 1 .$$
More precisely, for every $a>0$,
$$\int_{-a}^{a}\delta_n(x)\,dx \;=\;\frac 2\pi \arctan(na).$$

**Proof.** Fix $n\ge 1$ and let $F(x) := \dfrac 1 \pi \arctan(nx)$. By the chain rule and
$\dfrac{d}{du}\arctan u = \dfrac 1{1+u^2}$,
$$F'(x) \;=\; \frac 1\pi \cdot \frac{n}{1+n^2x^2} \;=\; \delta_n(x)$$
for all $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Hence by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (applicable since $\delta_n$ is continuous), for $a>0$,
$$\int_{-a}^{a}\delta_n(x)\,dx \;=\; F(a)-F(-a) \;=\;\frac1\pi\bigl(\arctan(na)-\arctan(-na)\bigr)
\;=\;\frac 2\pi\arctan(na),$$
using that $\arctan$ is odd. Since $\delta_n \ge 0$ and $\arctan(na) \to \frac\pi2$ as $a\to\infty$,
the improper integral converges and
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx \;=\;\lim_{a\to\infty}\frac2\pi\arctan(na)\;=\;\frac2\pi\cdot\frac\pi2\;=\;1. \qquad\blacksquare$$

## Lemma 2 (mass escaping from a neighbourhood of $0$)

For every $\eta>0$ and every $n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$,
$$\int_{|x| \ge \eta}\delta_n(x)\,dx \;=\; 1-\frac 2\pi\arctan(n\eta)\;=\;\frac2\pi\arctan\!\Bigl(\frac1{n\eta}\Bigr)\;\le\;\frac{2}{\pi n\eta},$$
and in particular $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{|x|\ge\eta}\delta_n(x)\,dx = 0$.

**Proof.** By Lemma 1, $\int_{|x|\ge\eta}\delta_n = \int_{-\infty}^\infty \delta_n - \int_{-\eta}^{\eta}\delta_n = 1-\frac2\pi\arctan(n\eta)$
(all three integrals being finite). For $t>0$ one has $\arctan t + \arctan(1/t) = \frac\pi2$, so
$1-\frac2\pi\arctan(n\eta) = \frac2\pi\bigl(\frac\pi2-\arctan(n\eta)\bigr)=\frac2\pi\arctan\frac1{n\eta}$.
Finally $\arctan u \le u$ for $u\ge0$ (both sides vanish at $0$ and $\frac{d}{du}\arctan u = \frac1{1+u^2}\le 1$), whence the bound $\frac2{\pi n\eta}$, which tends to $0$ as $n\to\infty$. $\blacksquare$

## Theorem

For every $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx \;=\;\phi(0).$$

**Proof.** Fix $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$ and set $M:=\|\phi\|_\infty<\infty$.

*Step 0 (the integrals exist).* $\delta_n\phi$ is continuous with compact support (contained in
$\operatorname{supp}\phi$), so $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \delta_n\phi$ exists and is finite. Also, the
function $x\mapsto \delta_n(x)\bigl(\phi(x)-\phi(0)\bigr)$ is continuous and dominated in absolute value
by $2M\,\delta_n(x)$, which is integrable over $\mathbb{R}$ by Lemma 1; hence it too is absolutely integrable
over $\mathbb{R}$.

*Step 1 (reduction).* Using Lemma 1 to write $\phi(0)=\phi(0)\int_{-\infty}^\infty\delta_n(x)\,dx$ and
linearity of the integral (legitimate by Step 0),
$$E_n \;:=\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx - \phi(0)
\;=\;\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\bigl(\phi(x)-\phi(0)\bigr)\,dx .$$
It suffices to prove $E_n\to 0$.

*Step 2 (splitting).* Let $\varepsilon>0$. Since $\phi$ is continuous at $0$, there is $\eta>0$ such that
$$|x|<\eta \;\Longrightarrow\; |\phi(x)-\phi(0)|<\frac\varepsilon 2 .$$
Split
$$E_n \;=\;\underbrace{\int_{|x|<\eta}\delta_n(x)\bigl(\phi(x)-\phi(0)\bigr)dx}_{=:A_n}
\;+\;\underbrace{\int_{|x|\ge\eta}\delta_n(x)\bigl(\phi(x)-\phi(0)\bigr)dx}_{=:B_n}.$$

*Step 3 (the inner part).* Since $\delta_n\ge 0$,
$$|A_n|\;\le\;\int_{|x|<\eta}\delta_n(x)\,|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\,dx
\;\le\;\frac\varepsilon2\int_{|x|<\eta}\delta_n(x)\,dx\;\le\;\frac\varepsilon2\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\,dx\;=\;\frac\varepsilon 2 ,$$
for every $n$, by Lemma 1.

*Step 4 (the outer part).* Since $|\phi(x)-\phi(0)|\le 2M$ everywhere,
$$|B_n|\;\le\;2M\int_{|x|\ge\eta}\delta_n(x)\,dx\;\le\;\frac{4M}{\pi n\eta}$$
by Lemma 2. Choose $N\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}$ with $N > \dfrac{8M}{\pi\eta\,\varepsilon}$ (possible by the Archimedean
property). Then for all $n\ge N$ we get $|B_n|\le \dfrac{4M}{\pi n \eta}<\dfrac\varepsilon2$.

*Conclusion.* For all $n\ge N$, $|E_n|\le|A_n|+|B_n|<\frac\varepsilon2+\frac\varepsilon2=\varepsilon$.
As $\varepsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $E_n\to0$, i.e.
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\delta_n(x)\phi(x)\,dx=\phi(0)=\delta(\phi).$$
Since $\phi\in\mathcal{D}(\mathbb{R})$ was arbitrary, $\delta_n\to\delta$ in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$, i.e. $(\delta_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}_{>0}}$
is a delta sequence. $\blacksquare$

## Remarks

1. The proof used only that $\phi$ is bounded, measurable, and continuous at $0$; smoothness and
   compact support were never used beyond guaranteeing these properties. Hence the same argument
   gives $\int_{-\infty}^\infty \delta_n \phi \to \phi(0)$ for every bounded continuous
   $\phi:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{C}$, a strictly stronger statement than convergence in $\mathcal{D}'(\mathbb{R})$.
2. An alternative route: the substitution $x=t/n$ turns $\int\delta_n\phi$ into
   $\frac1\pi\int_{-\infty}^\infty\frac{\phi(t/n)}{1+t^2}\,dt$; since
   $|\phi(t/n)/(1+t^2)|\le M/(1+t^2)\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ and $\phi(t/n)\to\phi(0)$ pointwise, dominated
   convergence gives the limit $\frac{\phi(0)}\pi\int\frac{dt}{1+t^2}=\phi(0)$. (The integrable
   envelope is essential here; pointwise convergence alone would not justify the interchange.)
